newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Economic gloom as Serbian protests mount.
newsitem.headline: Economic gloom as Serbian protests mount.

text.p: As protests against the Socialist rule of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic entered their fourth week, analysts said on Tuesday the country's economic future was gloomier than ever.
"The economic situation is completely chaotic. Nobody knows where this will end," Zoran Popov of the independent Belgrade Institute of Economics told Reuters.
Analysts said a sharp devaluation of the already weak Yugoslav dinar was now imminent, putting pressure on prices and reviving painful memories of the hyperinflation that swept the country in 1993.

"This would mean a huge inflationary push. You could expect some 100 to 200 percent inflation next year," Popov said. "But one devaluation is not going to be enough. You'll have to do it every three months and that will create an enormous crisis."

A harsh stabilisation programme stopped runaway inflation in 1994, but the currency quickly resumed its slide and the central bank devalued the dinar once again by some 70 percent in November 1995, pegging it at 3.3 to the German mark.

Amid growing political uncertainty created by the unprecedented wave of street protests, street dealers in Belgrade are now buying dinars at 3.7 to the mark. In other Serbian cities, marks are going at a rate of four dinars.

"The devaluation is already going on, slowly but steadily, and nobody can stop it," said Miroljab Labus, an economist at Belgrade University and deputy leader of the Democratic Party which is part of the Zajedno (Together) oppositon coalition.

A return to the economic chaos that embroiled Yugoslavia in the early nineties would be a catastrophe for the majority of the country's 11 million citizens, many of whom are already living hand-to-mouth and depend on food handouts for survival.
Average wages are barely a tenth of what they were before the country started its long descent into political and economic turmoil in 1991.
Per-capita output has dropped to less than $1,500 a year, putting Yugoslavia at the very bottom of the league of Europe's former East bloc nations.

Rising discontent over plummeting living standards in what was once the region's showpiece economy has added to the anger of up to 150,000 demonstrators who have taken to the streets of Belgrade for 22 days to demand the recognition of an opposition victory in November 17 municipal polls.
"The essence of this protest is to create a framework for change. We don't just want to oust Milosevic, we want a radical change of the economic and political situation," said Labus.

But economic reforms that would enable Yugoslavia to get the international credits it so desperately needs to revive its insolvent enterprises and obsolete infrastructure are a faint prospect in a society so closely controlled by a closely-knit Socialist elite that includes most state enterprises' managers.
"The reforms that we're now facing are painful. People don't understand that, they're afraid reforms will make their situation even worse," said Popov.

"Most of the state managers think we could continue to rely on our links with Eastern europe and Russia, implying this may be sufficient for a weak recovery. Rural people are inclined to trust this kind of ideology," he added.

Popov said even without access to western funds, the Yugoslav economy could tick over for another year or two by continuing to conclude barter deals with countries such as China or Russia and relying on several billions of dollars in savings that remain stashed away under citizens' mattresses.
"That way we could still manage to increase output by some seven percent next year, albeit from a very low base," he said. "This can't go on forever, but for a very long time."
What comes after that is anybody's guess.
"It's a gloomy prospect. I'm very afraid of our economic future," said Labus of the Democratic Party.
